# The difference in the data was real, but in practice not relevant

**Scenario (hypothetical):** A pilot air-cooling system will be installed on one London Underground line. To decide where, I analysed monthly average temperatures for each line from 2013 to 2024.

The dataset also includes the older "Sub-Surface Lines", which are built closer to the surface than the other lines. Because their conditions are not comparable with the deep-level lines, they were excluded from the analysis.

---

## Data Dictionary

The dataset variables are described in the table below:

Variable | Description
------------- | -------------
ID| Unique identifier for each observation (row) in the dataset
Year | Year of the data
Month| Month of the year
Line| London Underground Line
Temp| Temperature, measured in Celcius degrees

```{r setup, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(tidyverse)
options(width=100)
options(digits = 6)

```

## 1. General Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# First, read the data
underground <- read_csv("Underground.csv")

```

```{r echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Get a quick preview of variable structure. Verify data classes and size 
str(underground)

# Check descriptive statistics (Min, Max, Mean) 
# The Min. and Max. temperatures seem to be outliers or potential entry errors
summary(underground)

# All IDs are unique (disregarding missing values). Returns TRUE
n_distinct(na.omit(underground$ID)) == length(na.omit(underground$ID))

# Categories are unique and standardised
# All categorical variables (Year, Month, Line) show consistent frequencies, confirming the dataset is balanced. Every line has 12 years of monthly data, and every year/month is represented by all 8 lines
lapply(underground[c("Year", "Month", "Line")], table)

# Explore all records (rows) that contain at least one missing value (NA)
# 18 rows contain at least one missing value: 11 missing Temp and 7 missing ID
# 6 of the missing values are clustered on the Piccadilly Line, suggesting a systematic reporting issue for that line. The rest appear random across Year, Month, and Line
as.data.frame(
  underground %>%
    filter(rowSums(is.na(.)) > 0)
)

```

### a) Categorical Data Validation

```{r}

# Convert 'Month' to a factor with calendar sequence levels
underground_copy <- mutate(underground,
            Month = factor(Month,
              levels = c("January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June", "July", "August", "September", "October", "November", "December")))

# The seasonal trend (warmer in summer, colder in winter) confirms the data's general accuracy. However, outliers appear to be impacting the mean temperatures for March, April, July, August, and September
underground_copy %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarise(
    mean = round(mean(Temp, na.rm = TRUE), 2), 
    min = min(Temp, na.rm = TRUE), 
    max = max(Temp, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame()

```

### b) Visualisation of continuous variable "Temp"

```{r eda-plots, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Temp is right-skewed due to potential errors (values > 100.00°C) 
# There are also outliers visible near zero. 11 rows with Temp NAs are disregarded
ggplot(underground) + 
  geom_histogram(aes(x=Temp)) +
  labs(subtitle = "General Temperature (°C) distribution (all lines)")

# Low outliers (< 5.00°C) were observed on Bakerloo, Central, Northern, and Waterloo & City Lines. High outliers (> 100.00°C) were observed on Jubilee and Sub-surface Lines
# All identified outliers require investigation
# 11 rows with Temp NAs are disregarded
ggplot(underground) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Line, y = Temp)) +
  labs(subtitle = "Temperature (°C) distribution by line")

# Outliers analysis: extreme high values (206.30°C, 246.70°C) are physically impossible. Low outliers (< 5.00°C) are contextually implausible for the given months and statistically inconsistent with the monthly means (see Categorical Data Validation)
underground %>%
  filter(Temp > 100.00 | Temp < 5.00) %>%
as.data.frame()

# Excluding errors and outliers (17 rows) the general distribution (for all data) is nearly bell-shaped
# Data has multiple peaks, and is centered near 25.00°C
ggplot(underground, aes(x=Temp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.3) +
  xlim(10, 35) +
  labs(x ="Temperature", y ="Count", subtitle = "General Temperature (°C) distribution (all lines)")

# Histograms by line confirm the data is not normally distributed (errors, outliers, and NAs excluded)
# Most lines show multiple peaks, although Victoria's distribution appears the most symmetrical
ggplot(underground) + geom_histogram(aes(x = Temp, y=after_stat(density)), binwidth = 0.9) + 
  geom_density(aes(x = Temp), linewidth = 0.8) + facet_wrap(~ Line, scales='free_y', nrow = 2) +
  xlim(10, 35) + labs(y = "Density", x = "Temperature (°C)")   

```

### c) Data Cleaning

**Note:** A total of 17 records were excluded from the initial 1,152 (6 errors and 11 temperature NAs). The breakdown and justification for their removal are as follows:

- Errors: Records with a temperature above $100.00^\circ\text{C}$ or below $5.00^\circ\text{C}$ were removed due to their physical, contextual, and statistical implausibility.
- Temperature $\text{NA}$s: These were removed given the low volume (11 records), and as the majority appear random across Year, Month, and Line.

The subsequent analysis was performed on the remaining dataset. Records with missing $\text{IDs}$ but valid Temperature values were retained.

```{r}

# Remove missing temperatures (11 rows) and errors/outliers (6 rows)
underground_filtered <- underground_copy %>%
  filter(!is.na(Temp)) %>%
  filter(!(Temp > 100.00 | Temp < 5.00))

# Cleaned data rows check: 1152 - 11 NAs - 6 errors = 1135 records remain
nrow(underground_filtered)

```

### d) Data aggregation and reshaping

```{r, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Calculate the mean temperature, grouped by Year and Month (disregards NAs)
# Use month factor with calendar sequence levels [from (a) Categorical Data Validation]
underground_means <- underground_filtered %>%
  group_by(Year, Month) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean_Temp = round(mean(Temp, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
  )

# Reshape data to wide format for easier exploration
# Consistency of monthly temperature means across years confirms the stability and quality of the filtered data
underground_means %>%
  pivot_wider( #this function removes grouping (used in the previous step)
    names_from = Month,
    values_from = Mean_Temp
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame()

```


## 2. Summary table 

Summary table that shows the following for each London Underground line where temperature levels were measured: 

- The mean temperature
- The standard deviation of the temperature
- The lowest temperature recorded for that underground Line 
- The highest temperature recorded for that underground Line

```{r}

underground_filtered %>%
  group_by(Line) %>%
  summarise(mean=round(mean(Temp, na.rm = TRUE), 2), sd=round(sd(Temp, na.rm = TRUE), 2), min=min(Temp, na.rm = TRUE), max=max(Temp, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  as.data.frame()

```

**Note:** Bakerloo is the warmest line (Mean: 26.8°C), followed by Central (26.1°C) and Victoria (25.7°C). Among the three, Victoria has the highest temperature variation (SD: 3.19°C), followed by Central (SD: 2.86°C) and Bakerloo (SD: 2.61°C).

Removal of temperature NAs does not affect the interpretation of the warmest lines, as there were no temperature NAs found for Bakerloo, Central, or Victoria.


## 3. Excluding older London Underground Lines

The data set includes older London Underground Lines, these Lines are unusual in that they are built closer to the surface than the other lines – these are grouped together and called “Sub-Surface Lines”. These lines are excluded from the subsequent analysis.

```{r}

# Exclude the "Sub-surface_lines" data 
underground_filtered_final <- underground_filtered %>%
  filter(Line != "Sub-surface_lines")

# Verify removal of "Sub-surface_lines" data (144 rows). 
nrow(underground_filtered_final)

```

**Note:** New length is 993 instead of the expected 991 because 2 records (1 NA and 1 outlier/error) for "Sub-surface_lines" were removed in the prior Data Cleaning step.

## 4. Distribution of temperature across all years

The plot shows the temperature distribution for each line, with the mean (cross) and ± 1 standard deviation (blue bars).

```{r violin-by-line}
# Order lines for better comparison 
custom_line_order <- c(
  "Bakerloo", "Central", "Victoria", 
  "Northern", "Piccadilly", "Jubilee", 
  "Waterloo_and_City"
)

# Convert Line to an ordered factor
underground_filtered_final <- underground_filtered_final %>%
  mutate(
    Line = factor(Line, levels = custom_line_order)
  )

 # Create Violin Plot
temp_distribution_violin <- ggplot(underground_filtered_final, aes(x = Line, y = Temp)) +
  geom_violin(
    trim = FALSE,  # Prevents trimming the plot edges at the min/max data points
    fill = "#ADD8E6",  
    alpha = 0.7     
  ) +
  
  # Show the Mean (cross shape)
  stat_summary(
    fun = "mean",
    geom = "point",
    shape = 4,
    size = 3.5,
    color = "black" 
  ) +
  
  # Overlay Standard Deviation (Error bars, mean_sdl calculates Mean +/- SD)
   stat_summary(
    fun.data = "mean_sdl",
    fun.args = list(mult = 1),   # mean ± 1 SD (default is ± 2 SD)
    geom = "errorbar",
    width = 0.25,
    linewidth = 0.7,
    color = "blue"
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Temperature Distribution by Underground Line",
    y = "Temperature (°C)",
    x = "Line"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

print(temp_distribution_violin)

```

**Note:** The plot shows that most of the temperature distributions are asymmetrical (skewed). Temperatures cluster around two temperatures, a 'warmer' and 'colder' temperature average. 

The Bakerloo Line shows peaks around $29^\circ\text{C}$ and $25^\circ\text{C}$, and the Central Line shows peaks around $29^\circ\text{C}$ and $24^\circ\text{C}$. Given this non-normal distribution, it is better to check both the median and the mean for a representative measure of central tendency.

The Victoria Line shows the highest temperature variation (fluctuation around the mean), confirmed visually by the longest blue error bars (the mean $\pm \text{SD}$). Despite this high variation, the data for this line is relatively symmetrical, with the mean and median being close to one another.

```{r}
# Cohen's d: difference in means divided by the pooled standard deviation
# Rule of thumb: ~0.2 small, ~0.5 medium, ~0.8 large
cohens_d <- function(x, y) {
  nx <- length(x); ny <- length(y)
  sp <- sqrt(((nx - 1) * var(x) + (ny - 1) * var(y)) / (nx + ny - 2))
  (mean(x) - mean(y)) / sp
}

```

## 5. T-Test: Temperature Comparison (Bakerloo vs. Central)

A Welch t-test compares the mean temperature on the Bakerloo and Central lines.

```{r}

# Filter data to include only Bakerloo and Central Lines
BakerlooVsCentral <- underground_filtered_final %>%
  filter(
    Line %in% c("Bakerloo", "Central"),
  )

# T-test (excluding NAs, outliers/errors & Sub-Surface Lines) shows mean temperature in Bakerloo (26.82°C) is significantly higher than in Central (26.11°C). 
# The test is significant: t(281.6) = 2.18, p = 0.0303.
t.test(Temp ~ Line, data = BakerlooVsCentral)


# 95% CI of the difference (Bakerloo - Central) is included in the t.test output above
# Effect size
# Difference = 0.71°C, 95% CI [0.07, 1.35], Cohen’s d = 0.26 (small)
with(BakerlooVsCentral,
     cohens_d(Temp[Line == "Bakerloo"], Temp[Line == "Central"]))
```


## 6. T-Test: Summer Temperature, Bakerloo vs. Central

The same comparison, restricted to the summer months (May–August).

```{r}

# Filter data for Bakerloo and Central Lines during summer months (May-August)
BakerlooVsCentralSummer <- underground_filtered_final %>%
  filter(
    Line %in% c("Bakerloo", "Central"),
    Month %in% c("May", "June", "July", "August")
  )

# T-test (excluding errors/outliers & Sub-Surface Lines) shows mean temperature in Bakerloo (28.74°C) is not significantly different from Central (28.68°C) in summer. 
# The test is not significant: t(92.984) = 0.15803, p = 0.8748.
t.test(Temp ~ Line, data = BakerlooVsCentralSummer)

# Difference = 0.06°C, 95% CI [−0.69, 0.81], Cohen’s d = 0.03 (negligible)
with(BakerlooVsCentralSummer,
     cohens_d(Temp[Line == "Bakerloo"], Temp[Line == "Central"]))

```

## 7. Where does the difference come from?

```{r monthly-comparison, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
# Mean temperature by month for the two hottest lines
monthly_bc <- underground_filtered_final %>%
  filter(Line %in% c("Bakerloo", "Central")) %>%
  group_by(Month, Line) %>%
  summarise(mean_temp = mean(Temp), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(monthly_bc, aes(x = Month, y = mean_temp, colour = Line, group = Line)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 4.5, xmax = 8.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           alpha = 0.1, fill = "orange") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Bakerloo vs Central: mean temperature by month",
       subtitle = "Shaded area = summer (May-August)",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean temperature (°C)", colour = "Line") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

```{r outside-summer-ttest}
# Outside summer: is this where the yearly difference comes from?
BakerlooVsCentralRest <- BakerlooVsCentral %>%
  filter(!Month %in% c("May", "June", "July", "August"))

t.test(Temp ~ Line, data = BakerlooVsCentralRest)
with(BakerlooVsCentralRest,
     cohens_d(Temp[Line == "Bakerloo"], Temp[Line == "Central"]))
```

```{r summer-robustness}
# Robustness: does the summer conclusion depend on how "summer" is defined?
summer_defs <- list(
  "May-Aug" = c("May", "June", "July", "August"),
  "Jun-Sep" = c("June", "July", "August", "September"),
  "Jul-Sep" = c("July", "August", "September")
)

map_dfr(names(summer_defs), function(def) {
  d <- BakerlooVsCentral %>% filter(Month %in% summer_defs[[def]])
  t <- t.test(Temp ~ Line, data = d)
  tibble(summer = def,
         difference = round(unname(t$estimate[1] - t$estimate[2]), 2),
         ci_low = round(t$conf.int[1], 2),
         ci_high = round(t$conf.int[2], 2),
         p_value = round(t$p.value, 3))
})
```

Outside summer, Bakerloo is about 1°C warmer than Central (Cohen's d ≈ 0.4), which explains the yearly difference. In summer, when cooling is needed, the two lines are practically identical, regardless of how summer is defined.

# Summary of Findings
## Observation
The analysis utilised the provided dataset, which spans the period from 2013 to 2024 and initially contained 1,152 records. Errors and records from older lines were excluded, resulting in a final dataset of 993 records used for the analysis presented below.

## Conclusions
Both the average temperature (mean) and the middle temperature (median) were considered in this analysis. The median was given extra importance due to the observation that, for several underground lines, the temperature data is not evenly spread. Instead, it tends to cluster around two different common temperatures (a 'colder average' and 'warmer average' temperature). By focusing on the median as well, we gain a more robust view of the typical central temperature on a line.

Table 1 summarises the temperature statistics by underground line. The line with the highest overall median, mean, and maximum temperature was the **Bakerloo Line**. The **Central** and **Victoria** Lines also rank among the top three warmest lines. Among these three, the **Victoria** Line exhibits the highest temperature variability (standard deviation), followed by the Central Line.

```{r summary-table, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Create table with summary temperature statistics by line
mean_max_summary <- underground_filtered_final %>%
  group_by(Line) %>%
  summarise(
    Median_Temperature = median(Temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_Temperature = mean(Temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    Standard_Deviation = sd(Temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min_Temperature = min(Temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max_Temperature = max(Temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  mean_max_summary,
  col.names = c("Line", "Median (°C)", "Mean (°C)", "SD (°C)", "Min (°C)", "Max (°C)"),
  digits = 2,
  align = "lrrrrr",
  caption = "Table 1. Summary of General Metrics for Temperature by Line"
)
```

Figure 1 visually represents the distribution, mean, and median of the temperature data. The black boxes show where 50% of the temperature data points fall, with the thick horizontal black line indicating the median (midpoint). The blue 'X' marks the overall average (mean) for each line.

The Victoria Line stands out because it has the highest temperature fluctuation (variability).

```{r my-plot, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4} 
# Generate and format Figure 1
# Create and save plot to a variable
temp_distribution_plot <- ggplot(underground_filtered_final, aes(x = Line, y = Temp)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  # show the Mean (cross shape)
  stat_summary(
    fun = "mean",
    geom = "point",
    shape = 4, # Cross shape
    size = 3,
    color = "blue"
  ) +
  
  # Overlay Standard Deviation (the error bars)
   stat_summary(
    fun.data = "mean_sdl",
    fun.args = list(mult = 1),   # mean ± 1 SD
    geom = "errorbar",
    width = 0.2, 
    color = "blue"
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Temperature Distribution Across London Underground Lines",
    caption = "Figure 1. Comparison of Temperature Distributions Across London Underground Lines.",
    y = "Temperature (°C)",
    x = "Line"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.caption = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,         # Centers the text horizontally
      face = "italic"    
      # size = 10         
    )
  ) 

# Display the plot with the labels
print(temp_distribution_plot)
#print(final_plot_for_report)

```

A general $t$-test analysis comparing the mean temperature of the Bakerloo Line with the Central Line showed the mean temperature of the **Bakerloo** Line ($26.82^\circ\text{C}$) to be **statistically significantly higher** than that of the **Central** Line ($26.11^\circ\text{C}$), $\text{t}(281.6) = 2.18$, $\text{p} = 0.030$. However, the difference of $0.71^\circ\text{C}$ might be considered small for practical intervention. Furthermore, when analysing the **summer months (May to August)** specifically, the mean temperature difference is negligible: the Bakerloo Line ($28.74^\circ\text{C}$) is **not significantly different** from the Central Line ($28.68^\circ\text{C}$), $\text{t}(92.98) = 0.16$, $\text{p} = 0.875$.

The effect sizes confirm this: across the whole year the difference is small (Cohen's d = 0.26), and in summer it is negligible (d = 0.03). The monthly comparison shows that the yearly difference comes from the colder months, when Bakerloo is about 1°C warmer than Central. During the summer months, when a cooling system would actually be used, both lines reach practically the same temperatures, and this holds for alternative definitions of summer (June-September, July-September).

Based on the data, Bakerloo is a reasonable choice for the pilot, as it records the highest overall median (26.61°C), mean (26.82°C) and maximum temperature (32.41°C). However, the temperature data alone does not clearly separate Bakerloo from Central for the period that matters for cooling. The Victoria Line also deserves attention: it shows the highest variability (SD = 3.19°C), and its temperature peaks may contribute to passenger discomfort.

The decision should therefore be complemented with passenger volume per line: the expected impact of the system depends on both how hot a line gets and how many passengers are exposed to that heat.

```{r fig-articulo-setup, include=FALSE}
colores_lineas <- c("Bakerloo" = "#C4572B", "Central" = "#2F5D8A")

grados <- function(x) paste0(x, " °C")
```

```{r fig-articulo-1, include=FALSE}

etiquetas_lineas <- mensual %>% filter(mes == 12)

fig1_metro <- ggplot(mensual, aes(x = mes, y = temp, colour = Line)) +
```

```{r fig-articulo-3, include=FALSE}
ci_dif <- function(datos, etiqueta) {
  t <- t.test(Temp ~ Line, data = datos)
  tibble(periodo = etiqueta,
         dif = unname(t$estimate[1] - t$estimate[2]),
         li = t$conf.int[1],
         ls = t$conf.int[2])
}

diferencias <- bind_rows(
  ci_dif(BakerlooVsCentral, "Todo el año"),
  ci_dif(BakerlooVsCentralSummer, "Verano (may–ago)")
) %>%
  mutate(periodo = factor(periodo, levels = c("Verano (may–ago)", "Todo el año")))

fig3_metro <- ggplot(diferencias, aes(x = dif, y = periodo)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = li, xmax = ls), width = 0.15, linewidth = 1, colour = "#13233F") +
  geom_point(size = 3.5, colour = "#13233F") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%+.2f °C", dif)), vjust = -1.3, size = 4.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = grados) +
  labs(title = "La diferencia existe en el año, pero no en verano",
       subtitle = "Bakerloo menos Central: diferencia promedio y rango de valores compatibles con los datos (IC 95%)",
       caption = "Si el rango cruza la línea punteada (0 °C), no se puede descartar que no haya diferencia.",
       x = "Diferencia de temperatura (Bakerloo − Central)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey40"))

ggsave("fig3-diferencia-verano.png", fig3_metro, width = 9, height = 4.5, dpi = 200, bg = "white")
```
